docs.title: go-proc documentation
docs.text:
Pure-Go (CGO-free) process-lifecycle primitives — reap, supervise, respawn. A small family of dependency-free Go libraries, extracted and generalized from a microVM init, that answer the three questions any long-running init has to answer: who reaps the orphans, who keeps the workload up, and when should a crash actually restart.

Status: both primitives shipping

supervisor provides a PID-1 subreaper and a policy-driven process supervisor; respawn provides the debounce / anti-thrash / backoff decision core and its concurrent reconciler. Both are pure Go with CGO_ENABLED=0, dependency-free, at 100% coverage, and CI-green across the six 64-bit Go targets (amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x).

docs.title: The two primitives
docs.text:
Module Import path What it does supervisor github.com/go-proc/supervisor A subreaper (SIGCHLD + Wait4 on Linux, portable no-op stub elsewhere) that adopts and reaps orphaned children, plus a supervisor that drives a pluggable Runtime over a Spec of Procs and restarts each per its RestartPolicy (Never / OnFailure / Always), correlating every exit back to the process that owns it. respawn github.com/go-proc/respawn A restart / reconcile state machine: a pure Decide(policy, history, attempt, signal, now) → Plan core — grace-period debounce (anti-flap), max_restarts sliding-window anti-thrash, constant / exponential backoff — wrapped in a concurrent per-unit Reconciler driven by down / up / unhealthy / healthy signals through a caller-supplied Actions interface.

The two compose: supervisor owns the OS-level reaping and process running, while respawn owns the decision of whether and when a down process should come back. Either can be used on its own.

docs.title: Design in one line
docs.text:
supervisor reaps and runs; respawn decides.

The restart decision is a pure function of policy and history, so it is tested exhaustively without spawning a single process; the OS-facing reaper is isolated behind build-tagged files with fault-injection seams. See Why these primitives for the full rationale.

docs.title: Quick taste
docs.text:
supervisor — become a subreaper and supervise a spec:

stop := supervisor.StartReaper()   // Linux: PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER + SIGCHLD/Wait4
defer stop()                       // elsewhere: portable no-op

sup := supervisor.New(runtime, supervisor.Spec{
    Procs: []supervisor.Proc{
        {Name: "api", Restart: supervisor.Always},
        {Name: "batch", Restart: supervisor.OnFailure},
    },
})
sup.Run(ctx)                        // starts, watches, restarts per policy

respawn — decide whether a down unit should restart:

plan := respawn.Decide(policy, history, attempt, respawn.SignalDown, time.Now())
switch plan.Action {
case respawn.Restart:  // after plan.Delay (backoff)
case respawn.Debounce: // still inside the grace window
case respawn.GiveUp:   // max_restarts exceeded in the window
}

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0 — trivial cross-compilation, a single static binary, no C toolchain. Linux-only syscalls sit behind build tags with a portable no-op stub.
  • Mechanism, not policy engine. Reaping and running are separated from the restart decision; the decision is a pure, exhaustively-testable function.
  • Dependency-free. No third-party imports — only the standard library.
  • 100% test coverage is the target, enforced as a CI gate, error branches included.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Why these primitives — the reap / supervise / respawn split and why the decision core is a pure function.
  • supervisor — reap & supervise — the subreaper, Runtime, Spec, Proc, RestartPolicy.
  • respawn — restart state machine — Decide, Plan, backoff, the anti-thrash window, and the Reconciler.
  • Roadmap — what is shipping and what is out of scope.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome. go-proc is built to a small set of non-negotiable rules — they are what keep the primitives pure-Go, correct, and portable. Please read these before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Hard rules
docs.text:
• Build from source — no vendoring. Everything compiles from source. Do not reach for prebuilt binaries or vendored blobs as a shortcut; being able to compile from source is a guarantee of independence.
  • Pure Go, cgo disabled. The whole point is a single static binary with no C toolchain. Code must build with CGO_ENABLED=0. Linux-only syscalls (Wait4, subreaper prctl) go in build-tagged files with a portable no-op stub for every other GOOS — never a cgo shim.
  • Dependency-free. Only the standard library (and, on Linux, the low-level syscall surface). New third-party dependencies need a strong justification.
  • 100% test coverage target, enforced in CI. New code ships with tests, and coverage is a CI gate. Fill the error branches, not just the happy path — use the Runtime / Actions interfaces and the reaper stub as fault-injection seams.
  • Keep the decision pure. respawn.Decide must stay a pure function — no I/O, no goroutines, now passed in. Timing, concurrency and effects belong in the Reconciler / Actions, not the decision core.
  • All GitHub content in English. Issues, pull requests, commits, comments and discussions are English-only.
  • Six-arch clean. Changes must stay gofmt + go vet clean and green across amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le and s390x.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Pick or open an issue describing the change.
  2. Work test-first: add the unit tests (drive branches through the interfaces and injected now), then make them pass.

  3. Run the full suite with coverage and confirm the gate is green:

    COVERPKG=$(go list ./... | paste -sd, -)
go test -race -coverpkg="$COVERPKG" -coverprofile=cover.out ./...
go tool cover -func=cover.out | tail -1   # 100.0%

  4. Open a PR in English, referencing the issue.

docs.title: respawn — restart state machine
docs.text:
github.com/go-proc/respawn (package respawn) is a restart / reconcile state machine. Its core is a single pure function that decides whether — and when — a down unit should come back; that core is then wrapped in a concurrent, per-unit reconciler driven by liveness signals.

import "github.com/go-proc/respawn"

Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, dependency-free, 100% coverage, green on all six 64-bit Go arches.

docs.title: The pure core: Decide
docs.text:
plan := respawn.Decide(policy, history, attempt, signal, now)

Decide is a pure function — no I/O, no goroutines, and now is a parameter rather than a call to the clock — so its every branch is unit-tested against fixed inputs. It maps (policy, history, attempt, signal, now) to a Plan:

Plan.Action Meaning Restart bring the unit back, after Plan.Delay (the computed backoff) Debounce ignore for now — still inside the grace / anti-flap window GiveUp too many restarts in the sliding window; stop trying None nothing to do (e.g. a healthy/up signal for an already-up unit)

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
The state machine is driven by four signals:

  • down — the unit exited or was observed gone → candidate for restart.
  • up — the unit started successfully → resets the flap timer.
  • unhealthy — the unit is running but failing its health check → treated as a soft-down for reconciliation.
  • healthy — the unit passed its health check again → clears the unhealthy state.

docs.title: Anti-flap: grace-period debounce
docs.text: A unit that flaps down-up-down within a short grace period should not trigger a restart storm. Decide debounces: a down inside the grace window since the last up returns Debounce, not Restart. Only once the unit has been stably up past the grace period is a subsequent down treated as a real restart.

docs.title: Anti-thrash: max_restarts sliding window
docs.text: To stop a crash-loop from pinning a core, the policy carries a max_restarts budget over a sliding time window. Decide counts the restart timestamps in history that fall within [now - window, now]; if the budget is exhausted it returns GiveUp instead of Restart. Timestamps outside the window age out, so the budget continuously refreshes.

docs.title: Backoff: constant or exponential
docs.text:
When a restart is warranted, Plan.Delay is the backoff for this attempt:

  • constant — a fixed delay between attempts;
  • exponential — base × factor^attempt, clamped to a configured max, so successive failures wait progressively longer.

The attempt counter feeds the exponential curve; a successful up resets it.

docs.title: The concurrent wrapper: Reconciler
docs.text:
r := respawn.NewReconciler(policy, actions)
r.Signal(ctx, unit, respawn.SignalDown)   // feed events in

The Reconciler owns the per-unit state (history, attempt, last-up time), serializes signals for each unit, calls Decide, and then carries out the resulting Plan through a caller-supplied Actions interface:

type Actions interface {
    Start(ctx context.Context, unit string) error   // execute a Restart plan
    GiveUp(ctx context.Context, unit string)         // a unit exceeded its budget
}

Concurrency and effects live here; the logic lives in Decide. That separation is why the reconciler's plumbing and the decision rules can each be tested in isolation, and why the whole module reaches 100% coverage without timing flakes — the delay/window logic is exercised through injected now values, not real sleeps.

docs.title: Composing with supervisor
docs.text: supervisor answers "did this process exit, and who owned it?"; respawn answers "given that it's down, should it come back, and when?". A supervisor can hand each observed exit to a Reconciler as a down signal and let respawn own the debounce / anti-thrash / backoff decision, keeping the OS-facing reaper free of any restart policy.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• Pure decision core — Decide is a pure function of its arguments; now is passed in, so tests are deterministic.
  • Pure Go / CGO_ENABLED=0 — static binary, dependency-free.
  • 100% coverage including every debounce / give-up / backoff branch.
  • Six-arch clean — CI-green on amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x.

See Why these primitives for why the decision is deliberately a pure function separated from the reaper.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: go-proc is grown test-first: each capability ships with tests and a coverage gate rather than being built in isolation. Both primitives are shipping; the list below records what is done and what is deliberately out of scope.

docs.title: supervisor
docs.text: Stage What Status Subreaper (Linux) PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER + a SIGCHLD handler draining Wait4(-1, …, WNOHANG); orphans reaped, known PIDs routed to their owning Proc. Done Portable stub Build-tagged no-op StartReaper for macOS / Windows / other GOOS so the package builds, tests and hits 100% coverage everywhere. Done Spec / Proc / policy Spec of named Procs, each with a RestartPolicy (Never / OnFailure / Always); supervisor starts, watches and restarts per policy. Done Pluggable Runtime Runtime interface (Start / Stop) as the OS seam; fake runtime drives every restart / error branch deterministically. Done Exit correlation pid → Proc mapping so each exit reaches its owner and true orphans are dropped. Done

docs.title: respawn
docs.text: Stage What Status Pure Decide core Decide(policy, history, attempt, signal, now) → Plan; no I/O, now injected, every branch unit-tested. Done Anti-flap debounce Grace-period debounce of down signals inside the flap window. Done Anti-thrash window max_restarts sliding-window budget → GiveUp when exhausted, ages out over time. Done Backoff Constant and exponential (base × factor^attempt, clamped to max) delays. Done Concurrent Reconciler Per-unit state + serialized signals, carrying out plans through the caller's Actions interface. Done

docs.title: Documented out-of-scope boundaries
docs.text:
These are deliberate, recorded so each module's surface is unambiguous:

  • No process spawning inside respawn. respawn decides; it never starts or kills a process. Effects run through the caller's Actions — so the decision core stays pure and testable. Spawning is the Runtime/Actions implementer's job.
  • Subreaping is Linux-only by nature. On other platforms StartReaper is a no-op stub by design; go-proc does not emulate a subreaper where the OS has no such concept.
  • No supervision tree / dependency ordering (yet). Spec is a flat set of procs; ordered start-up and inter-proc dependencies are not modelled here.
  • No config-file format. Both modules are libraries with Go APIs; parsing a YAML/HCL unit file is a consumer concern layered on top.
  • No built-in health-check transport. respawn consumes unhealthy / healthy signals; how a caller probes health (HTTP, TCP, exec) is outside the module.

See supervisor and respawn for the shipping surfaces, and Why these primitives for the split.

docs.title: supervisor — reap & supervise
docs.text:
github.com/go-proc/supervisor (package supervisor) is two cooperating pieces: a PID-1 subreaper and a process supervisor. The reaper turns OS signals into exit facts; the supervisor drives a Spec of processes over a pluggable Runtime and restarts each per its RestartPolicy.

import "github.com/go-proc/supervisor"

Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0, dependency-free, 100% coverage, green on all six 64-bit Go arches.

docs.title: The subreaper
docs.text:
stop := supervisor.StartReaper()
defer stop()

On Linux, StartReaper marks the process as a child subreaper (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) so that orphaned descendants re-parent to it rather than to the real PID 1, then installs a SIGCHLD handler that drains exits with Wait4(-1, …, WNOHANG, …). Every reaped child's PID and wait-status is matched against the processes the supervisor started:

  • a known PID → the exit is delivered to the owning Proc, which applies its restart policy;
  • an unknown PID (a true orphan) → reaped and discarded, so no zombie ever accumulates.

On macOS, Windows and every other GOOS, StartReaper is a build-tagged no-op stub returning a no-op stop, so consumer code is identical everywhere and still compiles into a static binary. The subreaper behaviour is a Linux concept; the stub keeps the package portable.

stop() uninstalls the handler and restores prior signal handling — important for tests and for hosts that only want the reaper active for part of their lifetime.

docs.title: The supervisor
docs.text:
sup := supervisor.New(rt, supervisor.Spec{
    Procs: []supervisor.Proc{
        {Name: "api",   Restart: supervisor.Always},
        {Name: "batch", Restart: supervisor.OnFailure},
        {Name: "migrate", Restart: supervisor.Never},
    },
})
err := sup.Run(ctx)

docs.title: Spec and Proc
docs.text: A Spec is an ordered set of named Procs. Each Proc carries at least a Name and a RestartPolicy; the concrete command/args/env it represents is the Runtime's concern, keyed by name. The supervisor starts every proc, watches for its exit (via the reaper's exit facts), and consults the policy.

docs.title: RestartPolicy
docs.text:
Policy Restart on clean exit (status 0) Restart on failure (status ≠ 0) Never no no OnFailure no yes Always yes yes

OnFailure is the right default for one-shot-but-critical work (a migration that must succeed); Always for long-lived services that should never stay down; Never for genuine run-once tasks. Restart timing — backoff, anti-flap, anti-thrash — is not decided here; that is respawn's job, and the two compose.

docs.title: The Runtime seam
docs.text:
type Runtime interface {
    Start(ctx context.Context, p Proc) (pid int, err error)
    Stop(ctx context.Context, pid int) error
}

Runtime is the pluggable boundary between the supervisor's policy logic and the OS. In production it starts real processes; in tests a fake runtime returns scripted PIDs and exit statuses, which is how every restart branch — clean exit, failure, start error, stop error, context cancellation — is covered deterministically without forking. Correlating an exit back to the owning Proc is done by the PID the Runtime returned from Start.

docs.title: Exit correlation
docs.text: The reaper produces (pid, status); the supervisor holds a pid → Proc map from its Start calls. When an exit arrives it looks up the owner, records the outcome, and applies the policy. Orphan PIDs that were never in the map are reaped and dropped. This is what keeps a busy PID 1 zombie-free while still giving each supervised process an accurate view of its own lifecycle.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• Pure Go / CGO_ENABLED=0 — static binary, trivial cross-compilation.
  • Portable — Linux does real subreaping; other GOOS builds via a no-op stub.
  • Deterministically testable — the Runtime interface and the stubbed reaper give fault-injection seams for 100% branch coverage.
  • Six-arch clean — gofmt + go vet clean, CI-green on amd64, arm64, riscv64, loong64, ppc64le, s390x.

See respawn for the restart-timing decision that layers on top, and Why these primitives for the reap / supervise / respawn split.

docs.title: Why these primitives
docs.text:
Every long-running init or supervisor — a microVM PID 1, a container entrypoint, a service manager — has to answer three separate questions:

  1. Who reaps the orphans? When a process re-parents its children to PID 1 and then those children exit, someone must wait() on them or they become zombies forever.
  2. Who keeps the workload up? When a supervised process exits, someone must notice, correlate the exit to the right workload, and decide whether to run it again.
  3. When should a crash actually restart? Restarting immediately, always is how you get a crash-loop that pins a core. The real answer is a policy: debounce brief flaps, back off, and give up after too many restarts in a window.

go-proc splits these cleanly. supervisor owns questions 1 and 2 — the OS-facing reaping and the process running. respawn owns question 3 — the decision, as a pure function. The split is the whole point: it lets the tricky, timing-sensitive restart logic be tested exhaustively and deterministically, with no processes and no clock, while the syscall-bound reaper stays small and isolated.

docs.title: Reap: the subreaper
docs.text:
On Linux, supervisor.StartReaper() marks the current process as a child subreaper (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) and installs a SIGCHLD handler that loops Wait4(-1, …, WNOHANG, …) to harvest every exited child — both the processes it started and the orphans re-parented to it. Exits it recognizes are routed back to the supervisor so the owning Proc learns its child is gone; unknown PIDs (true orphans) are simply reaped and discarded.

The syscalls are Linux-only, so they live in build-tagged files (*_linux.go) with a portable no-op stub for every other GOOS. That is what lets the package build, test, and reach 100% coverage on macOS and Windows CI lanes while the real reaping is exercised on Linux.

The reaper is a mechanism. It has no opinion about restarts — it turns OS signals into "process N exited with status S" facts and hands them upward.

docs.title: Supervise: driving a spec over a pluggable runtime
docs.text: supervisor.New(runtime, spec) takes a Spec — a set of named Procs, each with its own RestartPolicy (Never, OnFailure, Always) — and a pluggable Runtime (the thing that actually starts and stops a process). It starts each proc, watches for exits via the reaper, and applies the policy. Because the Runtime is an interface, the same supervisor drives real OS processes in production and a fake, deterministic runtime in tests — no forking required to reach full branch coverage.

docs.title: Respawn: the decision is a pure function
docs.text:
The restart policy is deliberately not in supervisor. It is a standalone module, respawn, whose core is one pure function:

Decide(policy, history, attempt, signal, now) → Plan

Given the policy, the restart history, the current attempt, the incoming signal (down / up / unhealthy / healthy) and the current time, it returns a Plan: restart now, restart after a backoff Delay, debounce (still inside the grace window), or give up (too many restarts in the sliding window). No I/O, no goroutines, no wall-clock — now is a parameter — so every branch (anti-flap debounce, anti-thrash window, constant vs. exponential backoff) is unit-tested against fixed inputs.

That pure core is then wrapped in a concurrent, per-unit Reconciler that receives the real signals and calls a caller-supplied Actions interface to carry out the plan. The concurrency and the effects live in the reconciler; the logic lives in Decide, where it can be proven correct.

docs.title: Why pure Go matters here
docs.text:
Because both modules are CGO-free and dependency-free, they:

  • cross-compile to every Go target with no C toolchain, and link into a single static binary — exactly what an init that ships inside a microVM image needs;
  • carry no third-party dependencies — only the standard library and, on Linux, golang.org/x/sys-level syscalls behind build tags;
  • reach and hold 100% coverage including error branches, because the OS-facing parts are behind interfaces and stubs and the decision logic is a pure function.

See supervisor and respawn for the concrete surfaces.
